opening.headline: We solve the problem of users waiting because the response is too long and sending the response separately and notifying them later.
body: If the screen only shows a loading sign while the model produces a long answer, the user feels the service is stuck. Waiting for a long output through a single HTTP connection is also a burden on the server.

In this lesson, we'll look at streaming, which streams responses in pieces, a background mode where you can leave the work and receive results later, and webhooks, which notify you when it's done. At the end, we will check the criteria for choosing the method that suits the situation and the handling when a rejection arrives in the middle of the stream as an example.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the uses of streaming, background execution, and webhooks
You can choose an asynchronous method suitable for long-term work.

screens.title: Users leave due to long responses
screens.lead: As you select each item, the meaning of the scene unfolds. Look at the screen from the user's perspective and open it one by one.

visual.alt: A juxtaposition of an empty chat window, a loading indicator, and a bar showing the waiting time for the first letter to arrive.
labels: Waiting time until the first letter is visible
Couldn't the same response be delivered separately?

items.prompt: A user sent a question, but only a loading sign appears on the screen for several tens of seconds.
items.answer: The service is working, but the user can't tell. If you make the user wait in chunks for the response to be completed, it's easy for the user to feel stuck and leave the screen.

items.prompt: What kind of burden does it cause if you wait until the end of a long output with one connection?
items.answer: The longer the output, the longer you have to hold on to the connection, and if the connection is lost in the middle, you may miss out on the work you have done so far. This places a burden on both the server and the client.

items.prompt: So what questions will this class answer?
items.answer: How can the same response be divided or delivered at completely different times? The one in the front is streaming, and the one in the back is background mode and webhook.

screens.outro: If waiting is a problem, you need to change the way you arrive. First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Think about it: How to reduce waiting
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a service that shows part of a video or document first while downloading it?
items.answer: This is a method of showing the finished product first as it arrives, rather than waiting for it to arrive. It doesn't reduce the total time spent, but users feel progress. This is the principle behind streaming, where you receive the model response in pieces.

items.prompt: Which service took a long time to process and notified you of its completion via email or notification?
items.answer: This method notifies the user when it is finished rather than holding them in front of the screen. Batch jobs or report generation are common examples, and in the model API, background mode and webhooks take over this role.

items.prompt: Have you ever picked up work that was interrupted due to a lost connection?
items.answer: A method that requires maintaining the connection until the end is vulnerable to disconnection, while a method that leaves the connection to be viewed later is resistant to disconnection. Which one is right for you depends on whether the user wants to wait in front of the screen.

screens.outro: I will summarize the experiences I came up with under the names of server transmission events and webhooks. First, let's see how the stream arrives.

screens.title: What is a Server Sent Event (SSE)?
screens.lead: Below is a simplified example of what a Claude stream might look like arriving. Read the line-by-line description on the right to see how each event line is structured.

notes.note: If you put `stream: true` in your request, the response will arrive progressively as a server sent event. If this value is omitted, the response will only come in one complete chunk.

SSE is a method of keeping one HTTP connection open and having the server continuously push out events, and is defined in the standard (WHATWG HTML) as the format `text/event-stream`. Each event has a name line `event:` and a `data:` line, and the standard also has lines `id:` and `retry:`. The first message_start that arrives contains a Message object with empty content.

Characters are loaded in pieces in the content_block_delta event. The client simply glues these pieces onto the screen as they arrive. If you leave out pieces or join them out of order, the sentence will look broken.

By standard, events end with a blank line, and if the stream is interrupted without a blank line, the event is discarded. message_stop is an event that signals the end of the stream. If the connection is lost before receiving this event, the response is incomplete and should not be treated as complete. A standard SSE client can reconnect by placing the last event ID in the `Last-Event-ID` header, but reconnecting from the disconnection point varies from service to service, so you must follow the description of the corresponding API.

The official SDK provides a stream helper. By traversing `text_stream`, you can immediately print out the arriving letters, and if you only need the final message, you can receive the completed text through `get_final_message`. Useful for avoiding timeouts on large `max_tokens`.

screens.outro: Now that we understand what a line of events looks like, let's take a look at what types of events come in what order.

ext.title: WHATWG HTML Living Standard: Server-sent events

screens.title: Types and sequence of streaming events
screens.lead: Selecting a highlighted passage in the event sequence below will reveal its role in that event. Check them out in order from top to bottom.

visual.alt: A timeline with stream events laid out in order from left to right.
labels: index: Position of final content array

data.text:
1. message_start  
2. content_block_start  
3. content_block_delta (one or more)  
4. content_block_stop  
5. message_delta  
6. message_stop  
Midway: Ping events may be mixed, and if an error occurs, an error event may occur..

marks.note: This is the first event on the stream. A Message object with empty content arrives first and provides the framework of the response.
Signals the start of a block of content. The block's index corresponds to its position in the final content array.
A new fragment of the block content. If it is a text block, it contains the letters to be joined, and it arrives multiple times in one block.
Signals that the block has ended. A start, one or more deltas, and a stop make up a block of content.
Notifies changes at the top level of the message. For example, stop_reason arrives here.
This is the last event in the stream. The response is complete when you receive this event.

marks.span: Ping events may be mixed, and if an error occurs, an error event may occur.
marks.note: A ping is an event that can occur any number of times anywhere in the stream. Since it is not part of the response, you must be prepared to ensure that your processing code does not stop because of this event. In case of overload, an error event such as overloaded_error may come in the middle, so you must prepare a path for the client to process.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the normal flow, let's look at a case where a rejection occurs in the middle of the stream.

screens.title: Handling rejections while streaming
screens.lead: Let's take a step-by-step look at the processing sequence when a rejection arrives during a stream. Select the right arrow to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: 1. Recognize rejection signals
steps.body: When the streaming classifier detects a possible policy violation, the response `stop_reason` is `refusal`. Since rejection is not an error but a signal that arrives as a reason for termination of an HTTP 200 response, it is not revealed in monitoring that only looks at the error rate. You must manually enter the `stop_reason` test.

steps.title: 2. Read stop_details
steps.body: `stop_details` contains categories and explanations. In the event stream, this value arrives with stop_reason as message_delta. Note what type of rejection it was so you can use it for later analysis. The guidance text shown to users can also be selected based on this information.

steps.title: 3. Organizing the causal turns
steps.body: If you receive a rejection, you must reset the conversation context or remove or modify the causing turn. Otherwise, if you continue with the same history, the rejection will continue. In your server logic, place the process of reverting history as a required step in the rejection path.

steps.title: 4. Organize the letters you have already received
steps.body: Some texts you already received before rejection may be incomplete. Rather than leaving text piled up on the screen, organize the display and show instructions to the user.

steps.title: 5. Retry with organized history
steps.body: You can resume the conversation by sending a new request with your organized history. If you resubmit the same request to the same model, it will usually be rejected again. There are also ways to configure a server-side fallback or SDK middleware to retry with a different Claude model. It may be a good idea to instruct the user to change their request and try again.

screens.outro: Let's look at how, unlike streaming, the request itself is left to you.

screens.title: Background mode and webhooks
screens.lead: Compare the differences in how you alternate between the two states and see the results. Polling is a method where you go and ask, and a webhook is a method where the server notifies you.

visual.alt: Two diagrams comparing the arrow directions for polling flow and webhook flow.

states.label: polling
states.body: OpenAI background mode executes long-running tasks asynchronously by making requests to `background: true`. Developers poll the response object to check its status. The advantage is that the implementation is simple and you can ask questions at any time. As long as it is in the `queued` or `in_progress` state, it continues to query, and when it leaves that state, it has reached the final state. However, since we don't know when it will be completed, there is a cost for asking periodically. If you turn on `background` and `stream` together, you can remember the event's `sequence_number` as a cursor and resume the interrupted stream.

states.label: webhook
states.body: A webhook is a method that notifies the HTTP endpoint you operate when an event such as deployment completion or background response generation occurs. The response.completed event is used as an example. It's efficient because you'll be notified the moment it's completed without you having to ask. Since signature verification requires the raw text, the received text must be archived before parsing. Endpoints should respond quickly with a 2xx status code, leaving heavy processing to separate workers. If there is no response or a non-2xx response, OpenAI retransmits with exponential backoff for up to 72 hours, and in rare cases where the same event is delivered twice, it is filtered out with the `webhook-id` header. After receiving the notification, the results are searched using the event's response ID. OpenAI's webhooks follow the Standard Webhooks convention. In this protocol, a signature is created for values ​​such as `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, concatenated with raw text, and the recipient prevents replay attacks by rejecting timestamps that are outside the acceptable range. The protocol recommends treating `webhook-id` like an idempotent key, so you can just remember the ID you've already processed and skip duplicate events.

screens.outro: Now that I've seen all three methods, I'll explain which one is best for each situation.

screens.title: Commentary: Instant response screen vs report generation
screens.lead: The instructor takes turns explaining the two cases. Select the right arrow to follow the decision process.

visual.alt: A diagram with the two cases in the left and right columns and the selected method and decision basis summarized below.
labels: Case 2: Generating dozens of pages of reports
Basis for decision: Should users wait in front of the screen or receive results later?

steps.title: Examining Case 1
steps.body: This is the consultation chat window that the user is viewing. Users wait in front of the screen for an answer, and the first letter must be visible quickly for the conversation to be natural. If the completed answer comes late, you may drop out.

steps.title: Selection of Case 1
steps.body: In this case, SSE streaming is correct. The overall creation time is similar, but the first letter is visible faster, resulting in less perceived delay.

steps.title: Examining Case 2
steps.body: This function creates dozens of pages of reports. Users don't have to leave the screen on and can receive results later. It is a burden to hold on to a connection for such a long time.

steps.title: Choice of Case 2
steps.body: A design that starts in the background and is notified of completion via a webhook is appropriate. You can leave the request and hang up, and the server will notify you the moment it completes.

steps.title: Decision basis and limitations
steps.body: The criteria is whether the user can wait in front of the screen or receive the results later. Streaming must not be disconnected, and background requires status inquiry or webhook reception path. A design that mixes the two methods is possible, with the first part streaming and long follow-up tasks in the background.

screens.outro: Finally, let's look at situations where rejections arrive during the stream, both on screen and on the server.

screens.title: Explanation: Screen and server processing when a rejection occurs during a stream
screens.lead: Your instructor will explain what's happening on the screen and on the server, pairing them with the same steps. Select the right arrow to follow the steps.

steps.title: 1. Delta arrives and letters pile up
steps.body: Screen: The text from content_block_delta is attached to the chat window that the user sees. Server: Forwards events to the client as they are received. It is still in normal condition with no problems. Even in this section, the server continues to watch for a reason for termination.

steps.title: 2. Refusal arrives in message_delta
steps.body: The message_delta received by the server contains stop_reason: refusal. Since it is not a transient error, it should go through the reject processing route rather than retransmit.

steps.title: 3. The server records and excludes turns.
steps.body: The server records stop_details.category and excludes that turn from the conversation history. If you leave this in your history, your next request may be rejected for the same reason.

steps.title: 4. Organize the screen
steps.body: The screen will display a message such as “This request cannot be processed” and will clean up any text that has already accumulated. This is because the text you receive before rejection may be incomplete.

steps.title: 5. Continue with an organized history
steps.body: Subsequent requests are sent to the organized history. The user can continue with a new question, and the server will not reload the rejected question. Repeated rejections for the same reason can be tracked using the recorded categories.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: The delivery method is tailored to the user’s expectations.
screens.lead: The core of the class is gathered on one screen. Please read along with the questions asked at the beginning.

paragraphs: The first question was how the same response could be divided or delivered at different times. Streaming, which sends the response in pieces, reduces perceived delay, and background and webhooks, which leave the task to you and are notified of its completion, do not hold the connection.

Which one to choose depends on whether the user wants to wait in front of the screen or receive the results later. Even during streaming, rejections can arrive as stop_reason, so you need to prepare a path to organize the history and screen together.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Streaming is not a way to reduce total creation time, but rather a way to quickly display the first letter.

glossary.def: This is a server sent event. This is a transmission method that continuously pushes events to the HTTP connection opened by the server.
A streaming event that announces the arrival of a new piece of content block.
This is a method of executing long-running responses asynchronously and querying them later.
When an event occurs, the server notifies you to the HTTP address you set.
The termination reason indicates that the response was rejected due to policy.

misconceptions.myth: Streaming shortens the total creation time.
misconceptions.fact: The overall creation time is similar, it's just that the first letter appears faster. This is a way to reduce perceived delay.

If the endpoint fails to respond with 2xx, it will be retransmitted, and in rare cases, the same event may be delivered twice. Use the `webhook-id` header as the deduplication key, and after notification, query the results with the response ID.

misconceptions.myth: Rejection during stream is a general network error.
misconceptions.fact: A policy rejection is the response that arrives with stop_reason. To continue, the context needs to be cleaned up, and resending the same request won't fix it.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Streaming reduces perceived delay by fragmenting responses into server-sent events.
The Claude stream flows in the following order: message_start, content block start and delta and end, message_delta, message_stop.
Leave long-running tasks in background mode and check the status or be notified of completion through a webhook.
Even while streaming, rejections can come with stop_reason: refusal, so we clean up the context and try again.
Streaming is suitable for displaying screens immediately, and background and webhooks are suitable for generating reports.
